catalog_quote: There is a phoneme of stress. Intonation often makes it difficult to determine word stress because pitch is raised on the final syllable of a phrase. However, stress appears to be manifested by lengthening of the vowel when word stress is on an open penultimate syllable. new_statements.quote: There is a phoneme of stress. Intonation often makes it difficult to determine word stress because pitch is raised on the final syllable of a phrase. However, stress appears to be manifested by lengthening of the vowel when word stress is on an open penultimate syllable. [...] The clue may be that when the vowel in the penultimate is lengthened it receives the stress placement, since vowel length appears to occur only in stressed syllables; and when the penultimate is short, stress is on the final syllable. There is also secondary stress and there is length on the vowels of open syllables so stressed. Usually it appears that secondary stress is on the second syllable preceding primary stress, but sometimes it occurs three syllables before, particularly in verbs.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is phonemic (contrastive) and falls on either the penult or the final syllable; a stressed open penult carries vowel length, an unstressed (short) penult means final stress. Minimal pairs on p. 96: 'ba:lat 'banana' vs ba'lat 'broth'; '?u:tut 'rat' vs ?u'tut 'flatulence'; man'su:gob 'to quarrel' vs manso'gob 'to burn'. This is the standard Philippine penult/ultima contrast tied to penult vowel length.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress exists, with length on open syllables so stressed; usually on the second syllable before primary stress, sometimes the third syllable before, particularly in verbs (p. 96).
new_statements.exceptions: Author calls the analysis provisional ('Further study needs to be done on this whole subject'); phrase-final pitch raising obscures word stress; suffixation causes resyllabification and 'stress shift' (sec. 2, p. 98); /a/ reduces to [schwa] in unstressed syllables (sec. 1.3, p. 95).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (word stress), stated against phrase-level intonation (pitch raised on the final syllable of a phrase); citation-form words with stress and length marked.
new_statements.identity_note: Grayden 1979's data come from Mallango barrio, Tinglayan municipality (note 1, p. 99): 'The term "Southern Kalinga" refers to both the area of the said Municipality, and the dialect generally spoken' there, with minor inter-barrio differences and Butbut (Glottolog butb1235 [kyb]) as the chief divergent dialect. Mallango is an Ethnologue dialect of Southern Kalinga [ksc] alongside Bangad, Sumadel and Tinglayan, so the statement is for the Mallango dialect of sout2908 (Glottolog 5.1 label 'Bangad'), not specifically for the Bangad variety. The same PDF and stress statement were earlier filed under butb1235 as a sister-lect proxy; for sout2908 it is first-hand.

Word list p. 1 : every cited form checks (3. losán, 4. og-ót, 5. tíling, 6. sóngbat, 8. buwá, 10. dapúl, 11. odóg, 13. bálat, 14. úp-us, 15. man-amós, 17. túbun na buwá, 21. óbban, 24. úlos, 25. makúlap, 26. dála, 29. busáli, 35. mansogób; soggón, 36. ilobón, 37. ullápoy, 39. mangngína). Bangad 1973 : 2. al-algáw, 3. losán, 5. tiklíng, 6. sungbát, 13. bálat, 14. up-ús, 24. úlos, 25. kúlap, 35. sobgón, 36. ilobón, 37. ullápoy all as quoted; the NOTES line '/g/ tends to be unvoiced…
new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as Grayden 1979 (existing statement: contrastive stress on penult vs final): the same items appear with the same placement, e.g. bálat (Grayden's 'ba:lat 'banana' vs ba'lat 'broth') and mansogób (Grayden's manso'gob 'to burn'). Adds nothing on secondary stress or length. The catalog record's empty rule field can be filled from Grayden 1979 with these lists as corroboration.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The survey wordlists state no rule; they mark stress with an acute accent on each word (the Mallango list says so explicitly, the Bangad and Sumadel lists do it without comment). The marked position varies word by word between the penult (tíling, sóngbat, bálat, úlos, dála, ullápoy, mangngína) and the final syllable (losán, og-ót, dapúl, odóg, ilobón, sobgón/mansogób), i.e. stress is a lexical property, not fixed. Nothing on secondary stress; the Sumadel notes (p. 22a) and the Bangad notes cover only /d/, /l/, /b/, /g/ and the glottal stop.
new_statements.exceptions: Mallango compiler's caveat: the stress marks are 'not guaranteed to be entirely accurate'.
new_statements.identity_note: All three wordlists are from barangays of Tinglayan municipality (Bangad, Sumadel, Mallango), i.e. Southern Kalinga [ksc]; the Mallango list was written by Grayden's informant and Grayden 1979's data are from Mallango too. The 1980 vocabulary follows 'the dialect spoken in the northern half' of the Tinglayan area and notes minor north-south differences. The wordlists compare Southern Kalinga forms with Guinaang Kalinga (a different variety, 73.0% cognate per Pallesen), so Guinaang-based descriptions are not Southern Kalinga.
